html:
The 2010 Pakistan floods began in late July after very heavy monsoon rains and spread down the Indus basin over the next two months. About a fifth of Pakistan's land was under water at the peak.

The rains hit hardest in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where flash floods tore through valleys and caused most of the nearly 2,000 deaths. Then the flood wave moved south through Punjab and Sindh, breaking embankments and drowning farmland for weeks. Around twenty million people were affected, with homes, crops, livestock and roads lost.

The scale of the damage was one of the largest of any natural disaster of its time, and the slow rich world response drew criticism. The floods showed how much of Pakistan's life depends on the Indus and its canals, the system divided by the Indus Waters Treaty. Even worse floods came in the 2022 Pakistan floods, which put about a third of the country under water.
